draft.title: A significant Jewish practice
card: A Jewish practice is an action or ritual that Jews carry out as part of their faith. Practices express beliefs, so a ritual shows what the community holds to be true.
Synagogue service
communal prayer, with readings from the Torah scroll. It expresses the belief that God gave the Torah and that Jews are a community who pray and study together.
Marriage

the couple stand under a chuppah, a canopy that stands for the home they will build. Two witnesses are present, and the ketubah, a marriage contract, is signed. This expresses the belief that marriage is a sacred covenant with duties to each other.
Mourning
customs include a simple burial and shiva, a week when mourners stay together and receive visitors. They express respect for the dead and the community's duty to comfort the bereaved.
draft.remember: A Jewish practice is belief in action: each ritual expresses what the community holds to be true.

a.q: Why do the customs of shiva, where mourners stay at home and are visited, count as a Jewish practice that expresses belief?
opts: They show the community's duty to comfort the bereaved
They are a legal requirement of the Australian government
They are carried out only by rabbis on behalf of mourners
They replace the need for a burial after a death
a.why: Shiva is a ritual in which visitors comfort mourners, so it expresses a belief about duty to others in grief. It is not carried out only by rabbis: the mourners and the community take part.
a.clue: Think about what the visitors are doing for the mourners.

b.q: At Dana's wedding, the couple sign a ketubah and stand under a chuppah. Which belief does this ceremony most directly express?
opts: Marriage is a sacred covenant with duties to each other
Marriage is a private matter with no role for witnesses
Marriage is a contract that only the rabbi must honour
Marriage is a sign that the couple have left the community
b.why: The ketubah sets out the couple's duties to each other, and the chuppah stands for the home they will build together. The ceremony is not private or separate from the community, since witnesses are present and the couple's home is part of Jewish life.
b.clue: Consider what the signed contract sets out for the couple.

a.best: They show the community's duty to comfort the bereaved

b.best: Marriage is a sacred covenant with duties to each other

problems.detail: The card implies the ketubah sets out mutual duties. A traditional ketubah records the husband's obligations to his wife. Only some modern or egalitarian ketubot are mutual. The card should say this, or describe the duties more carefully.

The why says 'The ketubah sets out the couple's duties to each other', and the clue points students the same way. A traditional ketubah sets out the husband's obligations to the wife, so both overstate what the document says.

The distractors (an Australian legal requirement, replacing burial, done only by rabbis) are plainly absurd. The right option repeats the card's wording almost word for word, so the question is too easy for Year 12 HSC.

proposal.title: A significant Jewish practice
card: A Jewish practice is a ritual or action carried out as part of the faith. Each practice puts beliefs into action, such as beliefs about God, the Torah, covenant and community.
Synagogue service
communal prayer from the siddur, the prayer book, with readings from the Torah scroll. It expresses the belief that the Torah is God's teaching and that Jews worship and study as a community.
Marriage

the couple stand under a chuppah, a canopy that stands for their new home. A traditional ketubah, the marriage contract signed before two witnesses, records the husband's duties to his wife, such as providing for her. Some modern ketubot add promises both partners make. The ceremony expresses marriage as a sacred covenant.
Mourning

burial takes place soon after death, often in a plain coffin, to respect the body and show that all are equal in death. Then comes shiva, a week when mourners stay at home and the community visits to comfort them.
proposal.remember: Each ritual, from reading the Torah to sitting shiva, shows a belief being lived out.

a.q: Many Jewish families use a plain wooden coffin, whatever their wealth. Which belief does this mainly express?
opts: All people are equal in death
The body matters little once life has gone
Grief should be kept private within the family
Honouring the dead means spending generously
a.why: A plain coffin for everyone, rich or poor, shows that all are equal in death. It does not mean the body matters little: the quick, simple burial is a sign of respect for the body.
a.clue: Why would the rich and the poor use the same coffin?

b.q: At Eli and Ruth's Orthodox wedding, a traditional ketubah is signed before two witnesses. What does this document mainly record?
opts: The husband's duties to his wife
The equal promises each partner makes
The wife's duties to her husband
The rabbi's permission for the marriage
b.why: A traditional ketubah records the husband's obligations to his wife, such as providing for her. Equal promises from both partners appear only in some modern ketubot, not in the traditional form used here.
b.clue: The wedding uses the traditional form, not a modern one.
